lesson.title: Stimulus Generalization: When Similar Counts as the Same
lesson.summary: Stimulus generalization is the tendency for a conditioned response, once acquired, to also occur in reaction to stimuli that merely resemble the original conditioned stimulus.
lesson.body:
Learning would be inefficient if it only ever applied to the exact stimulus used during acquisition. In practice, once an organism has acquired a conditioned response to one stimulus, it tends to respond, at least to some degree, to other stimuli that are similar to it. That spillover is stimulus generalization, and the more similar the new stimulus is to the original conditioned stimulus, the stronger the response tends to be. Psychologists sometimes describe this pattern as a generalization gradient: response strength decreases smoothly as the new stimulus becomes less and less like the one used in training.

Pavlov saw this with his dogs as well. Once they had been conditioned to salivate to a tone of a particular pitch, they would also salivate, though somewhat less, to tones that were close in pitch to the original. A tone far removed from the training pitch produced little or no salivation at all. The dogs had not learned about one specific sound in isolation, they had learned something closer to a general category of sound.

Generalization is often adaptive. An animal that has learned a particular smell signals danger benefits from treating similar smells with at least some caution too, rather than requiring the exact same stimulus every time. But generalization can also cause problems when it spreads too far, producing a response to stimuli that genuinely have nothing to do with the original danger or reward. That is exactly the tension that discrimination learning resolves, and it is the natural next step after acquisition and generalization.
